query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as-deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloys, mesoscale chemical and defect heterogeneities create a broad distribution of local magnetic exchange interactions that control the magnetostructural transition, resulting in a sharp, hysteretic entropy change under low applied fields. A controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment that partially homogenizes the chemical order and relaxes local strains will reduce the spread of exchange parameters and, by promoting enhanced chemical short-range order, yield a broader and less hysteretic magnetocaloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloys produced by deposition processes that result in an ordered single‐phase hexagonal state with inherent mesoscale chemical and defect inhomogeneities.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, low-temperature thermal annealing treatment (performed below the full transition temperature) aimed at reducing local chemical heterogeneities and defect densities without causing major phase transformations.
generation.conditions: The annealing should be performed at a temperature moderately below the onset of irreversible phase changes relative to the magnetic transition and for a time calibrated to achieve partial homogenization. Tests should be conducted under low-applied magnetic field magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local chemical ordering/homogeneity and the density/distribution of defects (e.g., strained grain boundaries) that mediate the spread of magnetic exchange interactions.
generation.mechanism: Reducing local inhomogeneities narrows the distribution of exchange interactions, which, via enhanced chemical short-range order, transforms a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition into a broader, more reversible transition. This modification is expected to lower hysteresis losses and yield a magnetocaloric effect with an extended temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: After annealing, the alloy should exhibit a lower hysteresis (i.e. reduced loop shift/area in magnetic cycling) and a broadened (but slightly diminished peak) magnetic entropy change versus temperature compared to the as-deposited baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited alloy shows a sharp, hysteretic magnetocaloric response due to its inherent mesoscale chemical heterogeneity and defect-induced distribution of magnetic exchange energies.
generation.boundary: These predictions should hold for the specified non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi composition under low applied fields and within a moderate annealing temperature window; if the annealing treatment is too aggressive, unwanted phase changes may occur that would fall outside the expected behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing parameters (temperature and time) and the precise trade-off between maximum entropy change and decreased hysteresis remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy samples: one set remains as-deposited (control) and the other undergoes the controlled low-temperature annealing treatment. Subject both groups to low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles. Characterize the magnetic entropy change (ΔS) versus temperature and record the hysteresis behavior by measuring M(H) loops. Concurrently, use microstructural techniques (e.g., TEM, EDS) to assess the degree of chemical homogeneity and defect density.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change profile (ΔS vs temperature)
Hysteresis loop width and field shift during cycling
Microstructural analysis (grain boundary features, chemical homogeneity)
Magnetic exchange distribution indicators (from magnetometry data)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis and an appreciable broadening of the entropy change peak relative to the as-deposited samples (without any adverse effects from new phase formation), then the hypothesis that mesoscale chemical heterogeneities govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis would be falsified.

Changes in −ΔSmax as well as the changes in the shape of the −ΔS(ΔH, T) curves are important to MCE when applied to magnetic refrigeration, as they may lead to changes in the overall refrigerant capacity (RC). RC in general is the figure of merit used to compare MCE materials giving the total heat transfer of the material over a typical refrigeration cycle. RC for a given ΔH is calculated as the integral of −ΔS(T) over a temperature range of interest: Here, TR1 and TR2 are traditionally taken to be the temperatures corresponding to the FWHM of the −ΔS(T) feature on the low and high temperature sides of the peak, respectively. We do not consider hysteretic losses here, as the M(H) loops showed negligible hysteresis, though that can be important in many systems. Figure 5 shows RC as a function of ΔH for both the annealed and as-rolled samples. The RC of 36 J/kg for a 1 T field change puts these HEAs below many other materials designed to operate in the 100–200 K range, though several factors related to pragmatic engineering issues (e.g., ductility, corrosion resistance, high thermal conductivity) may make up for this.
